messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John is a 45-year-old European American male who works as a journalist. He has been married for over two decades and carries with him the heavy burden of a traumatic event that occurred during his captivity several years ago. The trauma has left deep scars both physically and mentally, and he continues to struggle daily with symptoms that have significantly impacted his life. John’s memories of captivity are vivid and recurrent, like an unwelcome film playing over and over again in his mind. He can still feel the terror that gripped him when unexpected or loud sounds would jolt him back into a state of high alert. The memory forces its way into his thoughts at the most inconvenient times, often without any apparent trigger. This replaying of traumatic memories is particularly distressing as it brings back the same overwhelming sense of fear he felt during captivity. The intensity of these memories has made John hyperalert to potential threats in his environment. He constantly scans for signs that might indicate danger, even when there is no real threat present. The slightest noise can send him into a state of panic, and he often reacts as if he were still in immediate danger. This hypervigilance has become a dominant feature of his daily life, affecting not only how he perceives the world but also how he interacts with it. John’s physical pain, particularly in his neck, serves as another trigger for these intrusive memories. The pain is often so intense that it brings back vivid recollections of the captivity ordeal. He has come to believe that any form of touch, even a gentle pat on the shoulder or hug from his wife, can ignite these painful memories and plunge him into a state of fear. The smell of alcohol also triggers John’s traumatic memories. This association is rooted in an incident during captivity when he was subjected to alcohol as part of his torment. Now, any whiff of alcohol serves as a stark reminder of that time, causing him to retreat from social situations where such smells might be present. His hypervigilance has led him to avoid certain environments and interactions that could potentially trigger these memories and associated physical reactions. For example, he often avoids going out with colleagues for drinks after work, which has strained his professional relationships. John's avoidance behaviors have also affected his personal life; he finds himself withdrawing from social gatherings where alcohol is present, leaving both him and his wife feeling isolated. John’s constant state of false alarms further exacerbates his hypervigilance and intrusive memories. Even when there are no actual threats present, he reacts as if danger lurks around every corner. This cycle of heightened alertness and memory replay has created a self-perpetuating loop that is increasingly difficult to break. The more frequently these triggers activate his traumatic memories, the more vigilant he becomes. John's struggles have become so intense that they are starting to interfere with his work as a journalist. His job often requires him to be in various environments where unexpected sounds and physical touch can occur. He finds himself unable to focus on his assignments due to the constant intrusion of these triggers and memories, which has led to missed deadlines and strained relationships with his editors. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer function normally without the constant fear and intrusive thoughts dominating his life. His wife had also noticed a significant change in him over the past few months, becoming increasingly concerned about his well-being and urging him to seek professional assistance. Despite these challenges, John hopes for a future where he can regain control of his life and be free from the relentless cycle of fear and trauma that has defined much of his recent existence.
